headline: Teenager's Thames Discovery Reveals London's Hidden Past
meta_description: 14-year-old Emmylou Vaxby has spent nearly a decade uncovering artifacts along the Thames foreshore, recently publishing a guide to mudlarking.
summary_short: A London schoolgirl has turned her childhood hobby into expertise, writing a published guide to mudlarking while uncovering centuries of the city's history.
body:
At just 14 years old, Emmylou Vaxby has become an expert in an unusual art form: mudlarking—the careful search for artifacts along riverbanks. Over nearly a decade, she has spent countless hours on the Thames foreshore near Wapping, discovering fragments of London's everyday past: clay tobacco pipes dating from the 16th century to the 1930s, cobalt-glazed Georgian or Victorian pottery, and shells from oysters to scallops. Her knowledge is so substantial that a publisher approached her to write a guide, and last summer she wrote between 1,000 and 2,800 words daily to complete A Guide to Mudlarking on the River Thames. The book is now published and available for £16.99.

Emmylou's passion began around age five or six during a casual outing with her friend's mother, but it deepened profoundly during the pandemic lockdown, when her entire family—both parents musicians and her younger brother—would spend their daily hour on the foreshore. What started as a personal interest evolved into public contribution: she began documenting her finds on a blog and YouTube channel under the name Emmylou the Mudlark, and in 2021, she founded the Wapping Plastic-Free Community through Surfers Against Sewage, organising twice-yearly riverbank clean-ups after witnessing a swan mistake plastic for food.

Beyond the historical treasures and environmental activism, mudlarking has become something more personal. Emmylou describes it as her "happy place"—an hour away from school stress, a meditative practice of careful observation where each discovery brings genuine satisfaction. One of her favourite finds is a pipe bowl made by 18th-century pipemaker William Manby, who lived nearby. Yet she remains grounded about the experience: "I get to do this for fun, while Victorian children would have to do this to make a livelihood." Her self-taught expertise and the freedom to pursue an unconventional passion have given her a remarkable self-assurance that extends far beyond the riverbank.
quick_facts: 14-year-old London schoolgirl explores Thames foreshore near Wapping
Nearly a decade of mudlarking discoveries: pottery, pipes, shells
Published A Guide to Mudlarking on the River Thames, £16.99
Founded Wapping Plastic-Free Community during pandemic lockdown
Finds include 18th-century pipe bowl by William Manby
